skyline.text: The made-up conspiracy theory that a lot of people believed
Why Russia’s Spain-sized economy cannot outlast the advanced world
The refusal to flee Kyiv that turned the war around

brief.head: Black and white
brief.text: You don’t invade your neighbours, Ajay Shah said. Claiming Russia may invade Ukraine over the treaties it wants is as preposterous as India invading Bangladesh over treaties. {014-C02}

brief.head: Narrative beats truth
brief.text: Ajay Shah found Russian propaganda on Indian outlets. Amit Varma blamed media’s shift from journalism to a content game, in which the best propaganda machines win. {014-C07}

brief.head: Not stuck in the mud
brief.text: Many expect the rasputitsa, the mud season, to halt the fighting. But the south is warmer than Kyiv, Ajay Shah said, and winter worsens Russia’s problems. {014-C17}

brief.head: The Finland tell
brief.text: Russia says it is fighting NATO. Yet with Finland now in NATO, Ajay Shah said, Russia’s force on the Finnish border has fallen from 100 units to 20. {014-S11}

brief.head: The lab of war
brief.text: Western armies have never fought a peer without air superiority, under skies full of enemy drones, Ajay Shah said. Now Ukraine knows more about conventional war than anyone. {014-C12}

thought.text: The chicken is involved, but the pig is committed.
thought.who: Amit Varma, recalling an old riddle about bacon and eggs to explain Ukraine’s morale

lead.kicker: Ajay Shah’s update on Ukraine, with Amit Varma
lead.head: No blitz, just a long squeeze
body: Ukraine’s summer counteroffensive has not produced the armoured breakthrough that American analysts hoped for, and many have called it a failure. Ajay Shah, back with Amit Varma for an update on the war, argued that they are watching the wrong game.

Varma began with the obvious question: why should India care about a war so far away? Shah’s answer was history. The defeat of Nazi Germany and the collapse of the USSR, he said, brought a great flowering of freedom, and Vladimir Putin wants to go back to a world where powerful countries invade their neighbours.

If Russia wins, Shah said, Belarus and Poland could be next, and China might make a play for Taiwan or India. “Liberal democracy is a fragile compact,” he said, “and we need to renew our vows every day.” {014-C01}
## Weak strongmen
Many in the Indian middle class, Shah said, respect strongmen and assume they build strong militaries. He argued the reverse.

In a liberal democracy, critics outside government find its mistakes and propose fixes. Militaries are harder to criticise, because of secrecy and patriotism. Under an authoritarian state the critics are silenced and nothing is disclosed.
“To understand a state is to understand that authoritarian countries make the worst militaries,” Shah said. {014-C05}
Varma saw the same rot in Russia’s failed invasion: an ageing autocrat surrounded by yes-men, his finest minds gone into exile, and delusions left unchallenged.
## The see-through battlefield

The battlefield has changed too, Shah said. The long-heralded revolution in military affairs is playing out fully in Ukraine, built on two things: drones, satellites and electronic monitoring that make the battlefield transparent, and precision munitions that land within 10 or 20 metres.

That ends the old doctrine of massing force in secret for a breakthrough. Shah asked listeners to “think of the footprint that 100 armored fighting vehicles and 1,000 people would leave in the eyes of a satellite”. {014-C09}
Western-style combined arms has a ceiling as well. Ukraine’s hastily trained civilians, Shah said, can make infantry, drones, artillery and tanks work together in groups of about 100, not 1,000.
So progress looks slow: by Shah’s count, Ukraine has crossed only about five of the 60 kilometres to the Sea of Azov.
## Grinding, not stalling

Attrition today, Shah argued, is not the trench stalemate of 1914 but Soviet-style deep operations. With NATO intelligence, partisans and standoff weapons such as Storm Shadow and HIMARS, Ukraine hits ammunition dumps, command posts and supply lines day after day.

Varma put it in chess terms. The Americans wanted Ukraine to attack like Tal or Fischer; Ukraine is playing like Capablanca or Karpov. “You can never say in advance what is going to break where,” he said, “but you have to just keep pinging away and something or the other will break.” {014-C15}

Ukraine’s real war economy, Shah said, is the whole advanced world, with South Korea the most important maker of the artillery shells it receives. Russia, with a Spain-sized GDP, loses about 1,000 tanks a year and makes about 200.
“Once you start thinking that wars are won by economies and not by militaries,” he said, “then it’s clear as day.” {014-C16}
So Ukraine can afford to waste equipment, but stays frugal with lives. The open question, Shah said, is whether Russia will find “Stalin levels of resolve” in coping with its losses.
His verdict on the counteroffensive was brief: “It ain’t done.”

second.label: Energy war
second.head: The gas bluff, called
second.deck: Ajay Shah on how Europe beat Russia’s energy blackmail, and what it cost Moscow
body: Vladimir Putin bet that cutting gas to Europe would cause a deep recession and working-class anger, feeding communists and Nazis and breaking Europe’s centrist coalitions. “We’ve seen that movie a hundred years ago,” Ajay Shah said.

Instead, Europe tripled its work on renewables, imported LNG from all over the world and protected poor households from the price rise. “Before the war, people believed that it takes two to three years to build an LNG terminal,” Shah said. “They got LNG terminals done in six months.” {014-S02}

Calling the bluff cost Russia its main buyer, Shah said, and its economy had been built on selling gas cheaply to Europe. {#gas} The advanced economies, he said, are easy to underestimate from a distance.

quote.text: There are going to be books and books written about how Europe fought that energy blackmail of 2022.

second.caption: how Europe beat the energy blackmail

third.head: Every front, all at once
body: After Operation Barbarossa in June 1941, Ajay Shah said, three German army groups advanced along a very long front in the USSR, towards St Petersburg, Moscow and later Stalingrad and the oil fields of Baku. {014-S08}

Stalin had to choose: mass his forces for one breakthrough, or fight in many places. Shah counts him, like Lenin and Trotsky, among the sophisticated intellectuals of the era. Stalin knew the USSR had the bigger population, and that with American industry behind it, it would outproduce Germany.
So he counter-attacked everywhere, to wear down German men and industry. Germany could not be strong everywhere, which is part of why it lost Stalingrad.
Shah’s summary: “You can’t predict where it will break, but it’ll break somewhere.” {#somewhere} That, he said, is the intuition for thinking about Ukraine today.
third.caption: Stalin’s choice not to concentrate

p2.title: The positional war
p2.deck: Ajay Shah and Amit Varma on why a slow counteroffensive is not a failed one

sections.label: Why it matters
sections.head: A faraway war, close to home
sections.caption: why a faraway war matters
body: Why should anyone in India care about a war in some other random place? Amit Varma put the question, and Ajay Shah answered with history.

The great drama of the 20th century, Shah said, ended with the collapse of Nazi Germany and the USSR, and a great flowering of freedom. Vladimir Putin seeks to go back to a world where powerful countries invade their neighbours.
Varma recalled Thomas Jefferson’s line that liberty requires eternal vigilance, and the hope captured by Francis Fukuyama’s essay *The End of History?*, which recent years have shaken. {014-R10}

The rise of Trump, Xi Jinping, Putin and Erdogan, Shah said, raises the stakes: right-wing authoritarians prop each other up, as Mussolini, Hitler and Imperial Japan did. Going upstream from Hemingway’s *For Whom the Bell Tolls*, he said, the world could not ignore Spain in 1936, and cannot ignore Ukraine now. {014-C01}
## The state is not the people

Varma urged listeners to separate Russia from the Russian people. Some 40 grandmasters, essentially the country’s top chess players, wrote a letter protesting against the invasion, and many had to leave Russia. The one exception he named, Sergey Karyakin, he called a coward. {014-S04}
For Shah, it was Garry Kasparov who showed him that Putin was not just one more Russian strongman. {#kasparov}
~ When a state invades another country, the hosts said, rallying around the flag is a basic intellectual blunder. Protest, Varma said, is the patriotic act.

quote.text: In my mind, there’s a simple line, which is you don’t invade your neighbors.

sections.label: The dark arts
sections.head: Yes-men make poor generals
sections.caption: why the invasion itself failed
body: Almost everyone, Amit Varma said, expected Russia’s invasion to succeed and its occupation to fail. As Michael Kofman put it in an interview Varma had read, the surprise was that the invasion itself failed.

The Russians had assumed they would be welcomed with open arms. Big armies, like big companies, can ossify and pass information slowly from bottom to top. And authoritarian leaders, Varma said, “get surrounded by yes men. And no one dares to contradict them in any way.” {014-C04}
Their finest minds go into exile, and delusions persist.
## Empire by stealth

Ajay Shah sees Vladimir Putin as a KGB man with a suspicious nationalism, who openly calls the USSR’s collapse a great geopolitical tragedy. Shah counts that collapse among the most glorious moments of the 20th century.

Putin is rebuilding an empire step by step, Shah said. Land is grabbed, fake republics such as the DPR and LPR are set up, and the Russian army fights in disguise in what is passed off as a civil war: the “standard Hitler-Stalin playbook”.
Behind it is the civilisational state, which rejects national borders. By that logic, Shah said, a state could claim the Chinese in Malaysia are oppressed and invade Malaysia to help them. {014-C03}
~ The borders between India and Bangladesh, and between China and India, are inviolable, Shah said.

quote.text: There is a phrase for it, it’s called civilizational state. The civilizational state is a truly dangerous concept.

sections.label: Incentives
sections.head: Ego versus existence
sections.caption: morale and authoritarian militaries
body: Amit Varma reached for an old riddle. When it comes to bacon and eggs, what is the difference between the chicken and the pig? “The chicken is involved, but the pig is committed.” {014-C08}
Russia, he said, is fighting for the delusions of one megalomaniac at the top. Ukraine is fighting for its existence.

Ajay Shah agreed that morale is an immense edge: war, he said, is about “money, men, material, and morale”. But Czechoslovakia and Austria were overrun all the same. You may fight as desperately as you can, Shah said, “but there are no guarantees”. {#guarantees}
## Three levels of trouble

Shah then set out three levels of governance. Civilian government in a liberal democracy is easiest: if everyone attacks the Bank of England every day, the bugs get fixed. Militaries are harder, because secrecy and patriotism mute criticism. Worst of all is the military of an authoritarian state, where critics are silenced and there is no market test.

The United States discloses how many artillery shells and Javelin missiles it bought in which year. “In the Indian budget, you get nothing,” Shah said. He finds Japan’s military easier to study than India’s.
~ Transparency, Varma added, indicates accountability, and accountability indicates efficiency. {014-C05}

quote.text: In the United States, you will get the precise fiscal data for how many artillery shells were produced in which year.

sections.label: The new warfare
sections.head: Aim at Andheri, hit Bandra
sections.caption: the revolution in military affairs
body: A tank on today’s battlefield, Amit Varma said, can be detected and destroyed within ten minutes. Ukraine was using about 10,000 drones a month, by older estimates, many of them cheap Chinese-made ones. {#drones}

Ajay Shah organised the history in phases: Napoleonic warfare; the First World War stalemate, broken by combined arms; the interwar work on tanks and aircraft by Marshal Tukhachevsky and German thinkers; then a long nuclear detour.
By the 1980s and 1990s people spoke of a revolution in military affairs, to the irritation of old-timers. In Ukraine, Shah said, it is playing out fully for the first time. {#rma}
## Thousands of bombs, one factory

It rests on battlefield transparency, from drones, satellites and electronic monitoring, and on precision. In the Second World War, half the bombs landed more than one or five kilometres from the target. {#bombs}
“So if someone tries to bomb me in Andheri,” Varma said, “they’ll get you in Bandra.” {014-J02}

Errors of 10 or 20 metres are now increasingly common, so force massed in secret can be seen and hit. Varma noted that one historian traces the American doctrine of concentrated force to Ulysses S. Grant. {014-J12}
~ The Americans expected Ukraine’s counteroffensive to fight that way, Varma said, and were disappointed when it did not.

quote.text: And all you need is 10 artillery shells with cluster munition to make a very bad day for that force.

sections.label: The front
sections.head: Too obvious to be the plan
sections.caption: the map, and the limits of combined arms
body: Ajay Shah walked listeners through the map. Without the Kerch Bridge, he said, Crimea has no land connection to Russia. {#kerch}

The occupied south is supplied out of Crimea, so every armchair strategist dreamt of one armoured thrust of about 60 to 65 kilometres to the Sea of Azov. Shah was suspicious. “If something is so obvious, you can’t be doing that.” {014-J07}

Amit Varma offered von Moltke and Mike Tyson on plans. Shah offered a borrowed line: “The plan is useless. The planning is everything.” What modern militaries need, he said, is “to be able to learn, improvise, and adapt under fire”. {014-C10}
## Two and two make twenty-two

Western combined arms asks infantry, drones, electronic warfare, artillery and tanks to work as one, which takes years of training and life-or-death trust. Pettiness gets in the way. The electronic warfare man, in Shah’s sketch, tells the drone man: “You guys, you just fly these birds. We shoot them down.” {014-J06}
Ukraine’s hastily trained civilians, Shah said, have managed it in groups of about 100, and fumbled above that. {014-C11}
~ Western doctrine also assumes total air superiority, he said, and has never faced enemy drones or a peer. Ukraine has.

quote.text: I think that war is the lab where the next generation of the Western way of war is being forged.

sections.label: The masterpiece
sections.head: Economies, not armies, win
sections.caption: the long war and its economics
body: America’s way of war, Ajay Shah said, was built around its industrial might and population. The giant slumbered until 1941, then built the world’s biggest tank factories from scratch. By early 1944, field commanders were saying they did not want any more tanks. {014-S06}

Churchill, leading a country with far fewer people to lose, kept holding the Americans back. History, Shah said, will judge him kindly. {014-S07} A smaller nation fights more cautiously, as Ukraine does with its soldiers.
## Quiet before the collapse

Ukraine’s gains at Kherson and Kharkiv also looked like fruitless attacks for a while, Shah said. Under the hood, Russia was losing its ability to supply Kherson, until one day it simply left. {014-S10}

The thrust to the Sea of Azov was really about logistics. HIMARS, with a range of about 30 kilometres, could not reach the M14 highway. Ukraine need only creep close enough, with better standoff weapons. {014-C14}
Shah dismissed Russia as “Saudi Arabia with nukes”, a Spain-sized economy facing the combined advanced world. {014-J05}
~ Even its force on the Finnish border, he said, has shrunk to a fifth of its traditional size.

quote.text: They’ve got to get close enough for their standoff weapons to disrupt Russian logistics. And that’s not as hard as it seems.

side.boxText: Ajay Shah calls Vladimir Putin a KGB man “brought up in the dark arts”, who sees the USSR’s collapse as a tragedy. Amit Varma saw in the failed invasion the megalomania of a 70-year-old who hankers for empire. {#megalomania}

contQuote.text: In fact, if our country does something wrong or if our government does something wrong, it is a sign of your patriotism that you protest for the sake of what your country means to you.

p3.title: War and other stories
p3.deck: Four tales told in the episode, from Kyiv to a manga master’s deathbed

stories.start: And so when Putin invaded uh Ukraine, actually they had not done
stories.end: And then the West started turning around and saying, No, I will support this.
stories.caption: Zelensky’s refusal to flee
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the moment the West changed its mind
stories.head: Offered a lift, he stayed put
body: Russia’s intelligence assessment, Ajay Shah said, was that a show of force would be enough. The West would buckle, and without Western support the Ukrainian army would flee. It would be like Afghanistan, where the Taliban won the moment the Americans left.

Vladimir Putin had his reasons. Russia invaded Georgia on 8 August 2008, and nobody helped. In February 2014 he grabbed Crimea, and nobody did anything. “And so he started getting comfortable that the West does not have a stomach for a fight,” Shah said. {014-S03}

Russia had not even done the full military planning for an invasion. Amit Varma recalled a clumsy landing at the airport in Kyiv, and different groups sent to assassinate Volodymyr Zelensky. “Thankfully they failed,” he said. {#assassins}
Then came what Shah called a priceless moment. The Americans offered Zelensky a flight out of Kyiv, exactly what they had done in Afghanistan.

“And Zelensky said, I don’t want a ride, I want ammunition,” Shah said. “That’s just one of the most priceless moments in world history, where he said, No, this is my country. I will stand and fight.” {014-S01}
Everything started changing around that, Shah said. Zelensky rallied his people, and the West turned around and said it would support Ukraine.
~ Shah likened it to 1939. Hitler had moved on Austria and Czechoslovakia, but when he invaded Poland on 1 September, England and France said enough is enough, and gave him an ultimatum to withdraw.
stories.why: Putin’s plan rested on an assumption about will: that nobody would stand and fight. One leader’s refusal to run broke it. Aggression that goes unpunished teaches the aggressor the wrong lesson, and appeasement tends to end abruptly.

stories.start: Bakhmut is important because Bakhmut was conquered by Wagner
stories.end: So it locks up a significant Russian force there
stories.caption: the fighting retreat at Bakhmut
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on why Ukraine fought for Bakhmut
stories.head: Lost the town, broke Wagner
body: Bakhmut, which Ajay Shah called a dinky town of 70,000 people, was taken by Wagner. Simplistic thinking says Ukraine should have retreated early. Retreat to where? “Cities are where you do the defense,” Shah said. {#dinky}

So Ukraine fought a long fighting retreat. “By and large, Ukraine lost,” Shah said. “But in the process of losing, they inflicted so much damage upon Wagner that it triggered off the mutiny by Wagner.” {014-S09}

Like Stalingrad, Bakhmut became a symbol. Losing ground that Prigozhin and Utkin had conquered would be a PR disaster for Russia’s defence ministry, so it pours forces in to hold it, and Ukraine keeps pressing.
~ “So you’ve always got to count the exchange rate,” Shah said: how many tanks, and how many people, each side loses.
stories.why: A town lost can still be a battle won. Count the exchange rate of losses, not just kilometres gained, and watch for symbols: a place that becomes one can turn into a trap that drains the enemy.

stories.start: Have you heard of a guy called Peter Mackindo? No. So Peter McIndaugh
stories.end: go around in a van and give out flyers and all of that
stories.caption: the birds that aren’t real
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a conspiracy theory invented on purpose
stories.head: Never seen a baby pigeon?
body: Amit Varma asked Ajay Shah if he had heard of Peter McIndoe. Shah had not. At 23, Varma said, McIndoe decided as a public experiment to give birth to a conspiracy theory: birds aren’t real.
Decades ago, the theory went, the US government killed millions of birds and replaced them with robots that spy on civilians. Why do birds sit on power lines? They are recharging.
“Have you ever seen a baby pigeon?” Varma asked. “It’s because only adult pigeons are created in the factories.” {014-S05} And why do birds poop on people? To track them.
~ McIndoe knew it was untrue, but many people believed him. For three years he kept up the charade, driving around in a van and handing out flyers. {#van}
stories.why: Belief is easily manufactured: a made-up theory, a few mock proofs and a van full of flyers were enough for many people. Varma called it a delightful story, told after Shah described skies full of enemy drones.

stories.start: And Tatsumi himself of this book wrote Tezuka was like a god for me
stories.end: unfinished uh uh work out there, and it's just inspiring
stories.caption: Osamu Tezuka’s last words
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the manga master who drew to the end
stories.head: Let me work, said the master
body: “Tezuka was like a god for me,” wrote Yoshihiro Tatsumi of Osamu Tezuka, in a passage Amit Varma read out. {014-J18}

The young admirer went on to pioneer gekiga, dark urban stories that were a reaction against manga. The master, Varma said, was taken by it, championed the new form and, around 1970, wrote *Ode to Kirihito* in its spirit.

Tezuka worked constantly all his life. In 1989 he died of stomach cancer. In hospital he kept trying to draw, and a nurse came to take his drawing equipment away. “And his last words were, I’m begging you, let me work,” Varma said. {014-S12}
~ After his death, his daughter opened his drawer at home and found a whole bunch of unfinished work. Varma found it inspiring.
stories.why: A master humble enough to learn from a young admirer, and devoted to his craft to his hospital bed. Varma, recommending *Ode to Kirihito*, called it one of the most powerful graphic novels he has read. {014-R04}

quiz.q: What did Zelensky tell the Americans when they offered him a flight out of Kyiv?
quiz.a: He said he did not want a ride; he wanted ammunition.

quiz.q: In Ajay Shah’s war arithmetic, what multiplication factor does Russian incompetence apply?
quiz.a: About 0.33, which makes the two sides roughly equal in battle.

quiz.q: Above roughly what group size have Ukraine’s hastily trained forces fumbled at combined arms?
quiz.a: About 100 people; a thousand cannot yet be made to work together.

quiz.q: Before the war, how long was an LNG terminal thought to take, and how long did Europe take?
quiz.a: Two to three years was the belief; Europe did it in six months.

quiz.q: Which chess players did Amit Varma say Ukraine is playing like, rather than Tal or Fischer?
quiz.a: Capablanca and Karpov, the positional masters who wait for chances to appear.

quiz.q: What were Osamu Tezuka’s last words, as Amit Varma told the story?
quiz.a: “I’m begging you, let me work,” as a nurse came to take his equipment.
